title: From Ahmedabad's Gullies to New Jersey Kitchens: The Gujarati Women Feeding the NRI Dream, One Thepla at a Time
excerpt: Small home-kitchen businesses run by Gujarati women are vacuum-sealing authentic snacks for diaspora travellers, turning nostalgia into a booming cottage industry.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Gujarati women are transforming home cooking into a thriving cottage industry for the diaspora.
  • Vacuum-sealed snacks like thepla and khakhra are essential for Gujarati travelers abroad.
  • Trust and community networks drive these businesses, relying on word-of-mouth recommendations.
  • The industry caters to a growing demand for authentic regional foods among Indian-Americans.
  • Personal pickups ensure freshness, highlighting the importance of tradition in modern entrepreneurship.
Before every flight to the United States, there is a ritual that almost every Gujarati traveller knows. It doesn't happen at the airport. It happens in a narrow lane in Ahmedabad's Old City, or in a cloud kitchen tucked into a Mumbai apartment, where a woman — a *ben*, in Gujarati — is vacuum-sealing stacks of methi thepla, crisp khakhra, and freshly fried fafda into airtight bags. These aren't commercial products. There is no brand label, no marketing budget, no Instagram account. What there is, instead, is a WhatsApp group, a decades-old reputation, and a line of customers that stretches from Borivali to the Bay Area. ## A Lifeline in Plastic Wrap A growing network of Gujarati women entrepreneurs in Mumbai and Ahmedabad has turned home cooking into a full-fledged cottage industry, catering specifically to NRIs, students, and tech workers heading abroad. Their products — traditional Gujarati snacks built for travel — have become essential carry-on cargo for a diaspora that refuses to compromise on *ghar ka khaana*. "I've been carrying homemade Gujarati snacks on my trips to the US since 2017," one techie based in New Jersey told The Indian Eye. "These foods are not just cheap and healthy alternatives to expensive American vegetarian options — they're a nostalgic taste of home." The numbers tell the story. One Mumbai-based *ben* has expanded from a single kitchen to two cloud kitchen operations to keep up with demand. Order volumes spike during summer and holiday travel seasons, when families place bulk orders for relatives overseas. The customer base now spans the US, UK, France, and Australia. ## The Economics of Nostalgia What makes this model work is trust. These businesses run entirely on word-of-mouth and community networks — the Gujarati equivalent of Yelp is an aunty's recommendation. Customers prefer personal pickup to ensure freshness, and many have been ordering from the same kitchen for years. The products themselves are engineered for diaspora life. Theplas made with extra oil and methi (fenugreek) stay fresh for weeks. Khakhras are naturally shelf-stable. Everything is vacuum-sealed, and some businesses have started nitrogen-packing for even longer shelf life — six to nine months without preservatives, no artificial colours. The margins are modest, but the volume is relentless. Some home kitchens produce upwards of 250 theplas and 100 rotis per week, charging rates that undercut any restaurant. Pani puri shells go for as little as $10 per 100 pieces. ## From Cottage to Cloud What was once a neighbourhood side hustle is professionalising rapidly. Brands like Surat-based Madhi ni Khamni have taken the concept online, offering instant khaman and locho mixes alongside traditional snacks, all shipped internationally with the same vacuum-seal technology the home kitchens pioneered. In Ahmedabad's Old City, several women have formed informal cooperatives, pooling orders and sharing distribution channels. The model requires no formal business plan, no venture capital, and no technology beyond a smartphone and a vacuum sealer — yet it generates consistent income and fills a market gap that no industrial food company has managed to address. "Despite the rise of online convenience, many patrons still prefer personal pickups to ensure freshness," notes The Indian Eye. It is a trust economy, built on reputation and flavour, not algorithms.

## More Than Food For the Gujarati diaspora, these vacuum-sealed packets carry something that no grocery store can stock: identity. The smell of thepla warming on a New Jersey kitchen counter is a bridge between continents. It tells a student eating alone in a shared apartment that home hasn't forgotten them. And for the women making it happen, the enterprise is equally meaningful. Many started cooking for neighbours out of necessity — a night-shift husband, children to support, no formal employment options. What they found was that the skills their mothers taught them had real market value, both locally and across oceans. ## The Diaspora Connection This micro-industry sits at the intersection of women's entrepreneurship, diaspora food culture, and the uniquely Gujarati talent for turning any skill into a business. It's a reminder that the Indian dream in America is sustained not just by H-1B visas and startup funding, but by a grandmother's recipe and a vacuum sealer. As one customer put it: "From home kitchens to global tables, Gujarati bens are feeding and fuelling the American dream."

## What's Next As the Indian-American population continues to grow — now the largest Asian-American group in several US states — demand for authentic regional home-cooked food is only going to increase. The question is whether these micro-enterprises can scale without losing what makes them special: the personal touch, the trust, and the taste of someone's mother's kitchen.
